title: Short Stuff: Does singing make you happy?
summary: Short Stuff episode on whether singing makes you happy. Chuck describes his interest in starting a neighborhood choir in his warehouse-style space with a piano, and the hosts note that roughly 29 million Americans regularly sing in choral groups. They discuss dance as a dementia-protective participatory activity, karaoke and confidence, and the physical benefits of singing as aerobic breathing that improves circulation and resembles meditation. They cite an Australian 2008 study finding choral singers more satisfied with life, a 1998 study where nursing home residents' anxiety and depression dropped after a singing program, and an English study of British choral singers. They cover how learning new music works the brain and offers a break from stress, and how belonging to a group is the biggest benefit of choral singing. The episode closes with Chuck's memory of hearing a choir sing a Radiohead song from a pier during a choral festival in Madison.

segments.title: Opening banter and choir idea
segments.summary: Chuck describes humanist choirs he saw on Instagram and his idea to start a neighborhood sing-along with a piano. Josh notes about 29 million Americans regularly sing in choral groups.

segments.title: Dance, karaoke and singing in public
segments.summary: Chuck mentions a study finding dance helps stave off dementia more than other participatory activities. The hosts discuss karaoke as evidence people enjoy singing in front of others, and note singing alone still brings benefits.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Short break before the main discussion.

segments.title: Confidence, endorphins and Australian choral singers
segments.summary: Chuck says singing releases endorphins and builds confidence. Josh cites a 2008 Australian study finding choral singers more satisfied with life than the general public, even after controlling for differences, and the hosts joke about Australian happiness.

segments.title: Nursing home and British choral singer studies
segments.summary: Chuck describes a 1998 study where nursing home residents in a singing program had decreases in anxiety and depression. He also cites a study of 600 British choral singers finding singing central to their psychological health. Josh asks about Ireland and Wales, and Chuck says the study did not look at that deeply.

segments.title: Physical benefits of singing
segments.summary: Josh explains singing is essentially aerobic because deep breathing increases oxygen in the blood and improves circulation. Singing is prescribed in lung rehab, and it resembles meditation-style controlled breathing.

segments.title: Chuck's sing therapy and learning new songs
segments.summary: Chuck shares that he sang loudly along to a player piano during a stressful period as a form of sing therapy, and Josh suggests learning new songs for brain benefits. Chuck adds that choral concentration on one's part takes attention off everyday stress.

segments.title: Belonging to a group
segments.summary: Josh says the biggest reason choral singing has the most benefits is belonging to a group, where each member is needed. Chuck recalls hearing a choir sing a Radiohead song from a pier during a choral festival in Madison.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the Madison story and wrap up the short episode, followed by the iHeartRadio production credit.
